co_east_side.blurb: A granite sport crag on the east side of the canyon above Lemon Reservoir, northeast of Durango. Granite is a change of pace in a region better known for sandstone and limestone. Nearly everything here is bolted, with just a couple of trad lines, and the grades run hard: the bulk fall between 5.10 and 5.13, with 5.11 and 5.12 the most common. The wall is low at its start and gains height as you move upstream, and the tallest stretch holds Brady's Route and Holy Grail. The cliff gets shade in the morning and sun later in the day, and the forested, high-elevation setting keeps summer days pleasant.
co_east_side.parking_note: Follow the forest road straight ahead from the gate at the north end of the reservoir, near Florida Campground. After roughly half a mile a big open gravel quarry sits on the left; leave the car there.
co_east_side.approach: A climbers' path leaves the north end of the quarry and winds through trees up to the base of the cliff.

co_easter_rock.blurb: A small, shady sport crag in Boulder Canyon, west of Boulder, whose walls face east and north. The rock is vertical to slightly overhanging and rewards power more than finesse. Almost all of the climbing is hard: most routes sit between 5.11 and 5.13, with 5.12 the most common grade, and only a handful of easier ones, plus two lines that take gear. Empire of the Fenceless and Tell-Tale Heart are the types of lines people come for. The cliff stays fairly shaded through the day and parts of it can stay dry in a light rain. Watch for loose rock, and expect a short, steep, brushy scramble up from the road.

co_nomad_s_cave.blurb: A steep, overhanging cave high up Clear Creek Canyon, west of Golden, just upstream of Primo Wall. It is a training ground for strong climbers: the roped routes are mostly hard sport lines in the 5.12 to 5.14 range, such as Freaks and Geeks, and the bouldering inside runs from V8 up into the double digits. Some holds are drilled pockets and others are natural. The overhang keeps the cave dry in the rain and cool in summer, but winter here is cold. Most people warm up on easier walls nearby before stepping into the cave.
co_nomad_s_cave.parking_note: Pull into the large turnout on the north side of US-6 just beyond Tunnel 6, about 11.3 miles up the canyon. A cable crossing over the creek is often rigged right there.

co_sno_cone_cave_the.blurb: A small, steep cave of limestone in Rifle Mountain Park, about a mile up the canyon from its mouth and just across the stream from the Arsenal. Every route is bolted, and the grades cluster from 5.10 through 5.13, with a few easier lines on the jumbled walls beside the cave. Bling It On and Fluff Boy are two of the better-known lines. It is smaller than most Rifle caves, and the spot is quiet and away from the road and the busier walls. The reeds you walk through on the way in are full of ticks in spring.
co_sno_cone_cave_the.parking_note: Leave the car in the shaded picnic area on the right, or at the big pullout beside the stream.

co_rincon_l_of_center_route.blurb: The left-of-center part of the Rincon wall in Eldorado Canyon, a small cliff with an outstanding density of high-quality traditional lines. Nearly all routes here are trad, with only a few bolts, so bring a full rack and the skills to place it. Most grades fall from 5.10 to 5.13, with 5.11 the most common, so it is a place for confident leaders; Over the Hill is a good lower-end option, while The Evictor and Aerospace sit higher up the scale. Expect company on nice weekends. Views stretch to the Continental Divide, and the descent is by rappel or by downclimbing gullies at either side.
co_rincon_l_of_center_route.approach: Take the Rincon trail from the west end of the canyon and hop up the talus field to the base of the wall.

co_south_park_3.blurb: A section of the Ouray Ice Park, the man-made ice climbing park strung along almost two miles of the Uncompahgre Gorge just outside the town of Ouray. Volunteers spray water from pipes on the rim to grow the ice, so routes build reliably through the winter. In this stretch, nearly all the climbs are water ice, mostly WI3 with a good number of WI4, and a couple of mixed lines such as Frenchy. Cartman's Mom, Fingerbang and Pinkeye are among the better ones. Popular parts of the park can be busy on winter weekends, and the ice is often rebuilt late in the day.

co_loch_vale_uphill.blurb: A high-country collection of ice and mixed routes in Rocky Mountain National Park, around 10,000 feet, on faces above Loch Vale and Mills Lake such as Thatchtop, Cathedral Wall and Powell Peak. These are longer, more serious days than the roadside ice nearby: most grades are WI4 to WI5, with mixed lines from M3 up through M5 and harder. Necrophilia, Deep Freeze and The Petit Gully are among the standouts. Expect a long hike in, and whether you need snowshoes depends on snowpack. Ice quality varies with the weather, and sun-baked faces can lose their ice.
co_loch_vale_uphill.parking_note: Use the Glacier Gorge lot on Bear Lake Road, about a mile before the road ends at Bear Lake.
co_loch_vale_uphill.approach: Hike roughly three miles up the Glacier Gorge trail to the junction, then bear left for Mills Lake or right for Loch Vale, depending on the face.

co_main_crag_2.blurb: The largest cliff in the Crosier Mountain crags above Big Thompson Canyon, with the longest routes in the group. The rock is granite, with slabs, knobby faces, easy cracks, a hard roof crack and some steeper technical lines. Most climbs are trad or mixed bolts and gear, and the grades are friendly: lots of 5.9 and 5.10 with a good spread of 5.11, including Dragon Slayer and Levitation. The crags look south, so they are hot in summer and best in spring and fall, though a calm sunny winter day can work. A 60 meter rope is needed for most rappels. The hike in is long and cairn-marked.
co_main_crag_2.parking_note: Start at the Crosier Mountain trailhead on the south side of County Road 43, about six miles east of Glen Haven.
co_main_crag_2.approach: Follow the Crosier Mountain trail for roughly two miles, crossing a big meadow, then follow cairns up to the base near Squat Tower.

co_d_cactus_cliff_right_left_of_funkdeme.blurb: A stretch of the Cactus Cliff on Shelf Road, north of Canon City, with solid limestone sport climbing on a south-facing wall. Every route here is bolted, and the grades are approachable: most are 5.9 and 5.10, with a decent run of 5.12s above them. Oscar de la Cholla, La Temperatura de Shelf and Almost French are some of the favorites. The cliff soaks up the sun, which makes it a good winter and shoulder-season choice and a hot place in summer. Cactus Cliff as a whole is known for having something at nearly every grade.
co_d_cactus_cliff_right_left_of_funkdeme.parking_note: Leave the car in the day-use lot at The Bank campground rather than along Shelf Road, then walk from there.

co_arsenal_the.blurb: A big overhanging limestone cave in Rifle Mountain Park, about a mile up the canyon, and one of the best-known power-endurance venues in the park. All sport, and hard: most routes are 5.12 and 5.13, with a few 5.14s, such as The Colinator. The rock is solid despite its rough look, with pockets, cracks and chunky pinches, and the holds are big and friendly. Pump-O-Rama, Sprayathon and Pretty Hate Machine are well-loved lines. The cave works well in the evening. On summer days the air at this end of the canyon can be still and buggy.
co_arsenal_the.parking_note: Park right at the base of the routes in the cave itself, or use a pullout by the river a bit farther down the road.
